You will see this phrase written in two ways:

  • Cosy up — British English (UK, Australia, India, etc.)
  • Cozy up — American English (USA, Canada)

Both are correct. They mean exactly the same thing. The difference is only in spelling, not meaning.

The word "cosy" (or "cozy") originally describes a feeling of warmth, comfort, and snugness — like how you feel wrapped in a blanket on a cold night. Think of a small, warm, safe space. That is the heart of "cosy."

When you add "up" to it, you get a phrasal verb: "cosy up."

"To cosy up" means to settle into a warm, comfortable position — often by moving close to someone or something, pulling yourself together, and relaxing.

Examples:

  • "It was raining outside, so we cosied up on the sofa and watched a film."
  • "The cat cosied up near the heater."
  • "She cosied up under a thick blanket with a cup of tea."

The image here is simple: you are physically making yourself snug, warm, and comfortable. You curl up. You get close. You settle in.

You can also use "cosy up to" in this literal sense:

  • "The puppy cosied up to her owner for warmth."

Here, the puppy physically moved close to its owner — pressing against them to feel safe and warm.
Meaning 2: Getting Friendly (The Social Sense — and the More Important One)

This is where the phrase gets more interesting and is used far more often in everyday speech.

"To cosy up to someone" means to become unusually friendly or close to a person — but often with a hidden purpose. You are being warm and charming toward them because you want something from them: their approval, their help, their power, their money, their influence, or simply to stay in their good books.

The key detail here is motive. The friendliness is not necessarily fake, but it is calculated. The person is making an effort to get close to someone powerful, important, or useful to them.

Examples:

  • "He has been cosying up to the manager ever since the promotions were announced."

(He is being extra friendly to the manager because he wants the promotion.)

  • "The new student quickly cosied up to the most popular group in class."

(She made an effort to befriend the popular group so she could become part of them.)

  • "Several companies cosied up to the new government after the election, hoping for contracts."

(The companies tried to build a friendly relationship with the new government for business benefits.)

  • "Stop cosying up to the teacher — it won't change your grade."

(Stop trying to impress and win over the teacher with extra friendliness.)
The Tone: Is It Positive or Negative?

This depends on the context.

When talking about physical comfort — it is completely positive and warm. There is nothing suspicious about it.

When talking about the social sense — the tone is usually slightly negative or suspicious. It carries the suggestion that the friendliness is not purely genuine. It implies the person is being strategically friendly — trying to gain something.

It is not as harsh as "flattering someone dishonestly," but it is not entirely innocent either. It sits somewhere in between — it hints at insincerity, opportunism, or self-interest.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She made friends with her new colleague." — neutral, no judgment
  • "She cosied up to her new colleague." — suggests she had a reason, perhaps to gain something

Understanding related phrases will sharpen your understanding:

  • "Butter someone up" — to flatter someone to get a favour. Very close in meaning to "cosy up to," but "butter up" is more about flattery with words specifically.
  • "Suck up to someone" — informal and more negative. Means to behave in an excessively eager, flattering way to gain favour. Stronger and ruder than "cosy up."
  • "Ingratiate yourself with someone" — formal. Means to work to earn someone's approval or favour by doing things to please them. "Cosy up to" is the casual, everyday version of this.
  • "Snuggle up" — close in meaning to the physical sense of "cosy up." Means to press or curl up close to someone for warmth or affection.
  • "Cuddle up" — also similar physically. Means to hold someone close in a warm, affectionate way.

"Cosy up" is a phrasal verb.

  • In the physical sense, you can say "cosy up" on its own, or "cosy up to" + a person/thing.
    "Let's cosy up." ✅
    "Let's cosy up to the fire." ✅
  • In the social sense, you almost always need "to" + a person.
    "He is cosying up to the director." ✅
    "He is cosying up." ✅ (less common, but works if the context is clear)

Tense forms:

  • Present: "She cosies up to him."
  • Past: "She cosied up to him."
  • Present continuous: "She is cosying up to him."
  • Noun form: You can sometimes hear "cosying up" used as a noun phrase — "All this cosying up to the boss won't help you."

Imagine a cold night. You pull a blanket tightly around yourself, move close to a warm fireplace, and feel snug and safe. That physical image of getting close for comfort and warmth is the soul of this phrase.

Now take that same idea and move it to human relationships: getting close to a powerful person, wrapping yourself in their warmth and favour — that is "cosying up to someone."

The warmth is real. But in the social sense, the warmth has a purpose.

• Physical meaning: To make yourself warm, comfortable, and snug — often by moving close to someone or something.
  • Social meaning: To deliberately become friendly and close to someone, usually because you want something from them or want to be in their favour.
